original_value: Three dimensional (3D) imaging technology has been widely used for many applications, such as human–computer interactions, making industrial measurements, and dealing with cultural relics. However, existing active methods often require both large apertures of projector and camera to maximize light throughput, resulting in a shallow working volume in which projector and camera are simultaneously in focus. In this paper, we propose a novel method to extend the working range of the structured light 3D imaging system based on the focal stack. Specifically in the case of large depth variation scenes, we first adopted the gray code method for local, 3D shape measurement with multiple focal distance settings. Then we extracted the texture map of each focus position into a focal stack to generate a global coarse depth map. Under the guidance of the global coarse depth map, the high-quality 3D shape measurement of the overall scene was obtained by local, 3D shape-measurement fusion. To validate the method, we developed a prototype system that can perform high-quality measurements in the depth range of 400 mm with a measurement error of 0.08%.

result.paraphrase: Three-dimensional (3D) imaging technology has seen broad use in applications such as human-computer interaction, industrial measurement, and cultural relic handling. However, current active approaches often need both the projector and camera to have large apertures to maximize light throughput, which results in a shallow working volume where the projector and camera are simultaneously in focus. In this paper, we present a new focal-stack-based method for extending the working range of a structured-light 3D imaging system. For scenes with large depth variations, we first use the gray code method for local 3D shape measurement with multiple focus-distance settings. We then extract each focus position’s texture map into a focal stack to create a global coarse depth map. Guided by this coarse depth map, high-quality 3D shape measurement of the entire scene is achieved through fusion of local 3D measurements. To verify the method, we built a prototype system capable of high-quality measurements over a 400 mm depth range with a measurement error of 0.08%.
